title: Bug
full_review:
Adapted from an acclaimed off-Broadway play and directed by "The French Connection" and "The Exorcist" helmer William Friedkin, "Bug" (Lionsgate) ultimately veers from taut thriller to genre horror flick. The cast's commitment to their roles, however, is undeniable and results in intense, often gripping, performances. Unfortunately, by the third act, the narrative becomes overwrought and escalates to diminishing returns.

Depressed bar waitress Agnes (a deglamorized Ashley Judd) lives in a cheap motel, dreading the likely return of her abusive ex-husband, newly released ex-con Jerry (Harry Connick Jr.). Their shared history includes the devastating disappearance of their only child, a 6-year-old boy.

She seeks oblivion in partying with a lesbian colleague, R.C. (Lynn Collins), who brings a timid drifter named Peter (Michael Shannon) to Agnes' motel room to share drinks and drugs. When Peter claims to be asexual as well as homeless, Agnes allows him to sleep on the sofa.

The following day as Peter returns to her with muffins and coffee, a glowering Jerry is just leaving, having slapped Agnes around and threatening more of the same. Agnes begs Peter to stay and they go to bed, establishing an instantly fierce bond that only tightens when he claims her room is teeming with bugs and details a government conspiracy of monumental proportions against them.

The screenplay by Tracy Letts, based on his play, initially explores Agnes' vulnerability and Peter's accelerating paranoia with sensitivity, but goes beyond a psychological study of loneliness and loss to present paranoia as a contagious condition. Peter's terror of the bugs of which he wishes to rid himself leaps horrifically from his self-mutilation to gory, brutal violence when a doctor (Brian F. O'Byrne) arrives on the scene.

Director Friedkin's camera seeks out constant revelatory close-ups but fails to avoid a decidedly stage-bound look with most of the action confined to the motel room. Despite good supporting performances from Connick and Collins, the film implodes with a screeching, nihilistic ending that undermines any broader social and political implications that Peter's rantings suggest.

The film contains excessive gore and violence, constant rough language and profanity, a casual sex scene, full male and female nudity, recreational drug and alcohol abuse, same-sex kissing and suicidal behavior. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.
